questions.question: The price of a product increases by 10%, and its quantity demanded falls by 20%. Explain what this tells us about the price elasticity of demand and what the result means for the firm's revenue.

rubric.name: Elasticity interpretation
rubric.description: Correctly explains that elasticity is greater than 1 and demand is elastic.

rubric.name: Calculation/application
rubric.description: Uses the percentage changes correctly to interpret the approximate elasticity.

rubric.name: Revenue implication
rubric.description: Correctly explains the likely effect of the price increase on total revenue when demand is elastic.

responses.text: Elasticity is 20 divided by 10, so it is 2. Since it is greater than 1, demand is elastic. A price increase will reduce total revenue because quantity demanded falls proportionately more.
The elasticity is 2, which means demand is elastic. The firm should expect revenue to decrease because the fall in quantity is larger than the rise in price.
Elasticity is 0.5 because we divide the 10 percent price increase by the 20 percent quantity decrease. Therefore demand is inelastic and the firm should get more revenue from the higher price.
The price rises 10 percent and demand falls 20 percent, so the consumers are quite sensitive to price. Revenue will probably fall.
Elasticity is greater than 1 because quantity changes by more than price. The company loses some sales, but because the price is higher the total revenue will definitely increase.
PED is 2, so it is elastic. This means customers respond strongly to price changes. A 10 percent increase in price with a 20 percent decrease in quantity suggests revenue falls.

Demand is elastic since a 10 percent price increase causes quantity demanded to fall by 20 percent. The main idea is that quantity responds more than price, so I think the firm's revenue is likely to decrease.
Elasticity is 2. I know the demand is elastic, but I am not sure whether revenue rises or falls because the price itself is higher.

questions.question: A firm's total cost is ₹500 when it produces 10 units and ₹620 when it produces 12 units. Calculate the marginal cost of the additional units and explain what the result means for the firm's production decision.

rubric.name: Marginal cost calculation
rubric.description: Correctly calculates marginal cost as change in total cost divided by change in quantity.

rubric.name: Numerical interpretation
rubric.description: Correctly interprets marginal cost as the additional cost per extra unit.

rubric.name: Production decision
rubric.description: Connects marginal cost to the production decision without incorrectly treating total cost as the cost of one additional unit.

responses.text: The change in total cost is 620 minus 500, which is 120. Output increases by 2 units, so marginal cost is 120 divided by 2 = ₹60 per unit.
MC = change in cost divided by change in output = ₹120/2 = ₹60. This means each of the additional units costs the firm about ₹60 to produce.
The marginal cost is ₹620 because that is the total cost at 12 units. Therefore the firm has to earn more than ₹620 from the extra production.
I think marginal cost is ₹120 because the firm's cost increased by ₹120 when it produced two more units.
Marginal cost is ₹60 per additional unit. If the revenue from producing another unit is higher than the marginal cost, producing more can make sense.
The company spends ₹500 at 10 units and ₹620 at 12 units, so the extra cost is ₹120. Dividing by 2 gives ₹60 marginal cost.
The marginal cost should be ₹60. The firm can compare this with marginal revenue to decide whether additional production is worthwhile.
The cost goes up by ₹120, so I would say the marginal cost of increasing production is ₹120. Since the firm produces two extra units, I'm not sure whether we need to divide it.

questions.question: A student has two hours available to study. They can either revise Economics or complete a part-time paid task worth ₹400. Explain the opportunity cost of choosing to study Economics and why it is important for making a rational decision.

rubric.name: Opportunity cost concept
rubric.description: Correctly identifies opportunity cost as the value of the best alternative forgone.

rubric.name: Application to the scenario
rubric.description: Correctly identifies the ₹400 paid task as the relevant foregone alternative if it is the best available alternative.

rubric.name: Decision reasoning
rubric.description: Explains that a rational decision compares the benefits of studying Economics with the value of the opportunity forgone.

responses.text: The opportunity cost of studying Economics is the ₹400 income from the best alternative use of the two hours. The student should compare the expected benefit from studying with that ₹400.
Opportunity cost is what you give up when making a choice. Here, the student gives up the ₹400 they could earn from the paid task.
The opportunity cost is ₹400 because that is the value of the next best alternative. A rational choice depends on whether the benefit from studying is greater than what is sacrificed.
The opportunity cost is the two hours of time spent studying because that is what the student gives up.
The opportunity cost is both the two hours and the ₹400. Studying has a time cost and an income cost, so both are the opportunity cost.
The opportunity cost is ₹400. If studying helps the student perform much better in the exam, that benefit might make giving up the paid work worthwhile.
The opportunity cost is the paid job because the student decides to study instead. It is important because choices involve trade-offs.
Opportunity cost means the total cost of studying, so it includes the time, the money that could have been earned, and even the effort of studying.
